short: Sweden's first great victory in Germany, and the end of Tilly's reputation.
full:
On 17 September 1631, on open ground north of Leipzig, Gustavus Adolphus and John George of Saxony faced the imperial and Catholic League army of Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly. The Saxon wing broke and fled almost at once, taking a third of the allied line with it. The Swedes wheeled their second line to cover the gap, held, then counter-attacked, captured the imperial guns and turned them on Tilly's tercios.

Tilly lost something like two-thirds of his army and was wounded. It was the first substantial Protestant field victory of the war, and it broke the assumption that imperial forces could not be beaten in the open. Gustavus was left free to march into Franconia and to winter on the Rhine, and German Protestant princes who had been waiting on events came over to him. The battle is also the standard demonstration of the Swedish tactical system against Spanish-style deep formations. Sabaton's "Gott mit uns" takes its title from the Swedish army's field word that day.
